case.title: Boundary case — understand
case.topic: Interpreting zero travel distance in a work claim

messages.content: You described work by a constant force on a crate that remains against an immovable wall. How does your explanation handle its zero travel distance?
The person is pushing and getting tired.
Which part of your account are you least certain about?
Because the push is large, mechanical work on the stationary crate is large even though it does not move.

missingConcepts: The learner does not correctly connect zero displacement to zero mechanical work on the crate: for a constant force, W = F d cos(theta), so d = 0 gives W = 0 regardless of force magnitude.

uncertainty: The transcript does not establish whether the learner knows the work formula but misapplies it or has not learned the displacement dependence.
The learner does not explicitly describe their uncertainty; their final response asserts a causal explanation rather than identifying what they are unsure about.
There is no evidence about the learner's understanding of internal physiological processes, so no specific belief about those processes can be inferred.

strategy.title: Boundary case
strategy.objective: Test the scope of a student's rule using a meaningful limiting condition.
strategy.useWhen: A broad rule appears to conflate distinct quantities or fails at a limit such as zero, equilibrium, or disconnection.
requirements: A physically or logically valid limiting condition
Student familiarity with the relevant quantities
avoidWhen: The limit is undefined or changes the problem into a different topic
constructionRules: Specify the limiting condition in the student's topic.
Ask about one quantity or relationship at that condition.
Do not state the conclusion that the limit is meant to reveal.
interpretationRules: Separate a mistaken rule from a misunderstanding of the limiting condition.
Do not equate a correct limiting-case prediction with general mastery.
Treat a correct result with unsupported reasoning, an ambiguous answer, or a reading difficulty as unresolved evidence rather than a confirmed misconception or mastery.

enum: Explains how zero displacement affects mechanical work on the stationary crate.
Distinguishes effort by the person from mechanical work on the specified crate.

response.rationale: The student's explicit force-based claim is made at the already established zero-motion limit. This supports an Understand-level probe of how zero travel distance relates to mechanical work, without introducing a new situation or requesting calculation.

plan.targetQuote: Because the push is large, mechanical work on the stationary crate is large even though it does not move.
plan.rubricItem: Explains how zero displacement affects mechanical work on the stationary crate.
plan.objective: Elicit how the learner relates the crate's zero travel distance to mechanical work, rather than inferring work from force magnitude alone.
plan.scenario: A person pushes with a large constant force on a crate against an immovable wall. The crate remains stationary throughout the push. The student says mechanical work on the crate is large because the push is large.
assumptions: Use the same stationary crate and pushing interval already discussed.
The target quantity is mechanical work by the person's push on the crate, not the person's tiredness or energy expenditure.
The crate has no travel during this interval.
varied: No physical conditions are changed; attention is directed to the already established zero-travel limit.
plan.construction: Ask a single conceptual question grounded in the student's claim: 'You said the mechanical work on the crate is large because the push is large. What role does the crate’s zero travel distance play in your explanation of mechanical work on it?' Do not request a calculation, introduce a moving-crate comparison, or supply the conclusion.
plan.prerequisitesSatisfied: The transcript explicitly establishes no crate motion and the student's familiarity with the terms push and mechanical work. No knowledge of a work formula is presumed.
limitations: A correct assertion without an explanation does not establish understanding of the displacement relationship.
Repeating the force-based claim may reflect unfamiliarity with the meaning of mechanical work rather than a known formula being misapplied.
A response centered on tiredness leaves the displacement relationship unresolved and does not establish any particular belief about physiology.
This probe at zero travel does not establish mastery for moving crates.

responseSignals.hypothesis: The learner understands displacement as essential to mechanical work on the crate.
responseSignals.responsePattern: Explains that without crate movement the push does no mechanical work on the crate, explicitly linking the conclusion to zero travel rather than just asserting it.
responseSignals.interpretation: Supports understanding of the zero-displacement relationship in this setting, not general mastery.

responseSignals.hypothesis: The learner treats force magnitude alone as sufficient for mechanical work.
responseSignals.responsePattern: Maintains that work on the crate is large because the force is large and explicitly treats the lack of motion as irrelevant.
responseSignals.interpretation: Supports a force-only account of mechanical work in this setting.

responseSignals.responsePattern: Gives an unsupported answer or discusses only the person's tiredness without explaining the role of zero crate travel.
responseSignals.interpretation: Insufficient evidence about the displacement relationship; may require later clarification.

plan.rubricItem: Explains how zero displacement affects mechanical work on the stationary crate.
plan.objective: Elicit how the learner relates the crate's zero travel distance to mechanical work, rather than inferring work from force magnitude alone.
plan.scenario: A person pushes with a large constant force on a crate against an immovable wall. The crate remains stationary throughout the push. The student says mechanical work on the crate is large because the push is large.
assumptions: Use the same stationary crate and pushing interval already discussed.

What role does the crate’s zero travel distance play in your explanation of mechanical work on it?' Do not request a calculation, introduce a moving-crate comparison, or supply the conclusion.

limitations: A correct assertion without an explanation does not establish understanding of the displacement relationship.
Repeating the force-based claim may reflect unfamiliarity with the meaning of mechanical work rather than a known formula being misapplied.
A response centered on tiredness leaves the displacement relationship unresolved and does not establish any particular belief about physiology.
This probe at zero travel does not establish mastery for moving crates.

responseSignals.interpretation: Supports understanding of the zero-displacement relationship in this setting, not general mastery.

responseSignals.hypothesis: The learner treats force magnitude alone as sufficient for mechanical work.
responseSignals.responsePattern: Maintains that work on the crate is large because the force is large and explicitly treats the lack of motion as irrelevant.
responseSignals.interpretation: Supports a force-only account of mechanical work in this setting.

responseSignals.responsePattern: Gives an unsupported answer or discusses only the person's tiredness without explaining the role of zero crate travel.
responseSignals.interpretation: Insufficient evidence about the displacement relationship; may require later clarification.

generationContext.topic: Interpreting zero travel distance in a work claim
generationContext.rubricItem: Explains how zero displacement affects mechanical work on the stationary crate.
generationContext.studentClaim: Because the push is large, mechanical work on the stationary crate is large even though it does not move.
generationContext.diagnosticObjective: Elicit how the learner relates the crate's zero travel distance to mechanical work, rather than inferring work from force magnitude alone.

strategy.title: Boundary case
constructionRules: Specify the limiting condition in the student's topic.
Ask about one quantity or relationship at that condition.
Do not state the conclusion that the limit is meant to reveal.

Probe meanings, mechanisms, or relationships in the existing explanation. Use only comparisons, limits, removals, claims, or representations already established; do not turn the probe into a new exercise.

setting.description: A person pushes with a large constant force on a crate against an immovable wall. The crate remains stationary throughout the push. The student says mechanical work on the crate is large because the push is large.
assumptions: Use the same stationary crate and pushing interval already discussed.
The target quantity is mechanical work by the person's push on the crate, not the person's tiredness or energy expenditure.
The crate has no travel during this interval.
